Self-hosting

Configuration

WhatEverFi reads its settings from environment variables, normally kept in the .env file next to the Compose file.

Where settings live

Each service reads its settings when it starts, so restart the services that read a setting after changing it. .env.example (source checkout) and .env.images.example (published images) list the common ones with short notes.

Do not commit .env. Never put COMPOSIO_API_KEY, OpenRouter keys, or provider tokens in git, logs, or chat.

Settings with names you choose

The Compose files pass the API and worker only the settings each one reads, listed by name, rather than the whole .env. A setting whose name you choose, such as TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_<NAME> or PHOTON_PROJECT_ID_<NAME>, therefore needs its own line: add it under api and worker environment in an override file layered after the base file (and in RAKAZO_COMPOSE_FILE when the updater is enabled), with no value so Compose fills it from .env. install-images.sh names any .env setting that no container receives.

# docker-compose.override.yml
services:
  api:
    environment:
      TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_SUPPORT:
      TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET_TOKEN_SUPPORT:
  worker:
    environment:
      TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_SUPPORT:
      TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET_TOKEN_SUPPORT:

install-images.sh layers a docker-compose.override.yml next to it automatically. In your own commands, add -f docker-compose.override.yml after the base file.

Core settings

All of these are optional:

RAKAZO_EXTRA_AUTH_ORIGINS=   # extra origins allowed to sign in and call the API; see below
SIGNUPS_ENABLED=true
SIGNUP_ALLOWLIST=you@example.com,@company.com
SCIM_BEARER_TOKEN=        # lets your identity provider add and remove accounts; see self-host-accounts.md
SANDBOX_PROVIDER=docker   # or none, e2b, novita, daytona, createos, boat. Keep fake only for pnpm test.
AGENT_RUNTIME=pi          # Keep scripted only for pnpm test.
WAKEUP_DRIVER=graphile
SANDBOX_IDLE_MS=600000    # pause or stop after 10 minutes idle; 0 disables idle sleep
# Set 0 when self-hosting with Docker, where an idle computer costs nothing, to keep long-running apps and sessions up.
# E2B, CreateOS and Boat still apply their own timeouts.
COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_MS=7200000 # uptime cap for providers that bill while running; minimum 60000; 0 disables
COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_UNBILLED_MS=0 # uptime cap for providers that do not bill while running (Docker, Kubernetes, Incus); minimum 60000; 0 (default) disables; needs SANDBOX_IDLE_MS on
SANDBOX_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 # stop a shell command after 5 minutes
MAX_TOOL_CALLS_PER_TURN=  # optional Pi turn tool-call fuse; unset/0 = unlimited
RAKAZO_MESSAGE_USER_MAX_CHARS=500 # message_user length cap; narration stays at 500
BOT_MESSAGE_MAX_HOPS=6    # bot-to-bot messages one chain may carry before the next is refused
E2B_API_KEY=              # when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=e2b
NOVITA_API_KEY=           # when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=novita; build its template first
DAYTONA_API_KEY=          # when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=daytona
CREATEOS_SANDBOX_API_KEY= # when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=createos
BOAT_API_KEY=             # when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=boat

COMPUTER_TAKEOVER_TTL_MS (default 900000, 15 minutes) is how long a person’s takeover of a bot’s screen lasts before control expires.

MODEL_STREAM_MAX_RETRIES (0 to 5, default 1) retries a model stream that fails partway; more retries let long turns survive brief provider failures.

Model timeouts are configurable in milliseconds. Invalid or out-of-range values retain their defaults. Longer timeouts can help when several bots share a local inference server that queues requests. For RAKAZO_LOCAL_MODELS servers and compatible model connections added in the app, these settings are the only limits WhatEverFi applies, and a stream that is cut off names why in the run’s error details, such as terminated (other side closed). Built-in providers still drop a response after 5 minutes without data, and a proxy or load balancer in between may cut off a silent stream sooner.

  • MODEL_STREAM_TIMEOUT_MS (default 120000, range 1000–2147483647) is the time budget for retrying the same model. It also controls the wait for response headers when using the OpenAI Chat Completions, Responses or Codex API, Anthropic Messages, Mistral or Azure OpenAI. Other APIs, such as Google, Vertex AI, Bedrock and some routed models, use their own client timeouts.
  • MODEL_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS (default 180000, range 0–2147483647) bounds how long a started response may remain silent. Set it to 0 to disable WhatEverFi’s inactivity watchdog. Explicit request cancellation remains available. Disabling this protection can leave stalled requests waiting indefinitely if neither the provider nor the caller terminates them.
  • MODEL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS (default 30000, range 1000–300000) bounds connecting to an OpenAI-compatible model or speech connection added in the app. RAKAZO_LOCAL_MODELS servers and built-in providers retain Node’s own connection timeout.

Reaching WhatEverFi from a second address

Sign-in and API calls are accepted only from WEB_ORIGIN, API_URL, BETTER_AUTH_URL and the mobile app. If you also open the same install from another address, such as a Tailscale name or a LAN IP, the browser or desktop app gets 403 INVALID_ORIGIN. List that address in RAKAZO_EXTRA_AUTH_ORIGINS, comma-separated:

RAKAZO_EXTRA_AUTH_ORIGINS=https://rakazo.your-tailnet.ts.net,http://192.168.1.20:5173

Each entry must be a bare origin (scheme, host, optional port; no path). https:// is accepted for any host. http:// is accepted only for loopback, .local, and private-network IPs (RFC 1918 and Tailscale’s 100.64.0.0/10). Anything else is ignored and logged as a warning. Only origins you list are trusted; the default is none. WEB_ORIGIN stays the address used in links, passkeys and OAuth callbacks.

Feature switches

Variable Default Effect
TICKET_BOARD_ENABLED false Turns on the ticket board. Set it on the API and worker.
USER_DEVICES_ENABLED on false stops signed-in desktop apps from letting bots run commands on the user’s own computer. Set it on the API and worker.
PI_SESSION_RECORDING off true records agent sessions as JSONL under DATA_DIR/pi-sessions. The files are not encrypted, so do not use it on a shared or multi-tenant install.
PRIVACY_POLICY_URL WhatEverFi’s policy The privacy policy linked from the AI data-sharing notice. Set it on the API.

Database roles

WhatEverFi uses two Postgres logins:

  • The owner (POSTGRES_USER, or DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL outside Compose) runs migrations and owns the tables.
  • The app login (rakazo_app with POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD, or DATABASE_URL) is not a superuser, cannot bypass row-level security, cannot create objects, and can only read and write the app tables.

pnpm db:migrate (in containers, its prebuilt form pnpm --filter @rakazo/api db:deploy, which the one-shot migrate container runs before the API starts) applies the migrations and the job queue schema as the owner. Only that container gets the owner login, so code running in the API or worker cannot find one that bypasses row-level security. It then creates the app login named in DATABASE_URL, or updates its password, and grants it the rakazo_app role. When migrations run as a role without CREATEROLE, as on some managed Postgres, create the login yourself and GRANT rakazo_app TO <login>.

Messages, events, threads, memory, artifacts, secrets, model and voice credentials, skills, bots, runs, tasks, routines, connections, MCP servers and sign-ins, computers, boards and tickets, messaging identities and outbox, external conversations, steering messages, usage, scratchpad items and approval rules have row-level security. Each signed-in request sees only its Space’s rows, plus the user’s own account-level credentials. A query that leaves out its Space filter returns nothing from other Spaces. A background job that acts for one run, routine, computer, skill, thread or cloud agent runs as that row’s Space and user, so agent tools get the same backstop. Security events are written and read only in system scope. Reconcilers, queue sweeps, the messaging outbox drain and webhooks run in a named system scope (runAsSystem in packages/db). That scope also sends a key derived from the app login’s password, which pnpm db:migrate registers, so SQL that runs for one Space cannot switch itself into system scope. An app login without a password in DATABASE_URL has no key, and pnpm db:migrate warns. The job queue’s tables (graphile_worker) hold job metadata, not Space content: graphile-worker turns on row-level security for them, and pnpm db:migrate adds a policy that gives the app login every row.

With only DATABASE_URL set, migrations and the app share one login. Everything keeps working, but pnpm db:migrate, the API and the worker warn that row-level security is not enforced. To fix this, set DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL to the owner and DATABASE_URL to a new login.

Run pg_dump as the owner. The app login would only dump rows it is allowed to see.

Database connections

The API keeps a pool of 4 Postgres connections and the worker a pool of 8. DB_POOL_MAX sets both to the same value, so size it for the worker: Graphile Worker needs at least 6, and the worker also holds three listening connections and a leadership connection.

REALTIME_DATABASE_URL sends the long-lived LISTEN connections that carry live updates to a different address than DATABASE_URL, for example a direct connection when DATABASE_URL goes through a transaction pooler. It defaults to DATABASE_URL.

GRAPHILE_WORKER_CONCURRENCY (default 4) caps concurrent deliveries from the older interactive job queue during rolling upgrades. New agent runs dispatch straight from Postgres and do not take those slots.

API and worker memory

Chat runs execute in the API container that receives the message, and routines and other background runs execute in the worker, so both hold live agent turns. In the production Compose file, RAKAZO_API_MEMORY_LIMIT and RAKAZO_WORKER_MEMORY_LIMIT cap them (Compose sizes such as 2g or 3072m, default 2g each). Raise them on a larger host. Deploys briefly run the old and new container of each side by side, so leave room for both.

Postgres memory

The production Compose file sizes Postgres for an 8 GB host: POSTGRES_MEMORY_LIMIT caps the container (default 2560m), POSTGRES_SHARED_BUFFERS sets its cache (default 1GB, which counts against that cap) and POSTGRES_EFFECTIVE_CACHE_SIZE tells the planner how much data stays cached (default 2GB). On a smaller host, lower them along with the API and worker caps above. Changing them restarts Postgres.

Listening addresses

The API listens on API_HOST (default 127.0.0.1) and API_PORT (default 3100). Keep loopback unless a container or a trusted reverse proxy must reach it; the Compose files set this for you. The published-images stack publishes the web app on 127.0.0.1:5173 and the API on 127.0.0.1:3100; set RAKAZO_WEB_PORT or RAKAZO_API_PORT to use other host ports. For LAN access, set RAKAZO_WEB_BIND as described in Connecting a phone on the same network.

Outbound proxy

To send the API and worker’s outbound traffic through a corporate proxy, set HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY (either case works) in .env. List the stack’s own service names in NO_PROXY so internal traffic skips the proxy:

HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128
NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,postgres,supervisor,api,worker,web

For mirrors of the installer and images, see restricted networks.
